summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory. Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate across the parts of it under Moroccan control, and a visitor there stands under Moroccan law wherever those institutions act. Human Rights Watch recorded that authority in a dispatch of 9 December 2005, covering the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests; the organisation called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under that framework and carries six months to three years of imprisonment. The broad discretion police hold in applying morality provisions is the instrument turned on visibly trans people.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, a partially recognised state and an African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. Its own legal order is recorded by the Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA as punishing same-sex sexual activity for both males and females with up to three years of imprisonment, and a global legality roundup published in July 2017 lists the state as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, and illegal there for decades.

Protection machinery is absent on both sides of the dispute. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states that there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence, a conclusion it reaches in part from a 2010 statement by Ahmed Mulay Alli, the Sahrawi state's diplomatic representative in Mexico, that the constitution does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice and does not punish it. The statement resolves nothing for a visitor: the conduct is recorded as criminalised, while the protective text a traveller might rely on does not exist.

A visitor should expect screening, questioning and detention to be carried out by Moroccan officials in the controlled areas, under a morality provision whose wording leaves the decision to arrest largely with the officer on the street. No trans-specific entry rule, gender-marker rule or documented incident of trans-specific violence in the territory is recorded in the available sources.
tangentialFactors:
The territory's legal inheritance runs through Spain, which held it until 1976; homosexuality was not decriminalised in Spain until 1979, and the criminal provisions in force locally predate that reform rather than follow it.

Morocco occupies most of the territory the Sahrawi state claims, and same-sex activity is also illegal there, so the two frameworks a visitor might be measured against point in the same direction. The Sahrawi state's claim to the territory has been recognised by the African Union since 2016 without settling which courts and which penal code a person in the territory answers to.

Social conditions compound the legal position. Most residents are Muslim and same-sex relationships are seen as a foreign phenomenon, which narrows the room a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor has in public, markets and checkpoints well before any statute is invoked.

Official statements and practice diverge. The 2010 constitutional claim of non-punishment sits alongside a criminalisation record maintained by three separate rights monitors, and alongside a 2009 report finding that Sahrawi officials detained people on homosexuality charges. A traveller should treat the more restrictive reading as the operative one.
localsOnly:
Residents of the territory live under criminal provisions reaching three years of imprisonment for same-sex conduct under the Sahrawi framework, and six months to three years under the Moroccan penal framework applied in the controlled areas. The same police discretion over morality provisions that shapes a visitor's exposure is the daily instrument used against local LGBTQ people, including visibly trans residents.

CEAR records that no protection exists for LGBTQ individuals against discrimination or violence, which means a resident who is assaulted, dismissed from work or driven from a home has no complaint mechanism built into the legal order. The constitutional silence identified in 2010 does not create a right; it leaves the criminal provisions standing and the protective provisions absent.

Sahrawi human-rights defenders have been prosecuted for organising in the territory. The seven defenders tried on charges of fomenting illegal protests were from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, and the charges were disputed by Human Rights Watch, indicating that collective advocacy carries a prosecution risk independent of sexual-orientation law.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the available sources: no trans-specific rule on legal gender-marker change, passport or ID presentation at entry, bathroom and facility access, hate-crime enhancement, or access to hormone care is recorded for Western Sahara. Any statement about those questions would be unsourced.

The 2009 USCRI finding that Sahrawi government officials running refugee camps were holding some prisoners on homosexuality charges, in cases where the alleged facts would more fittingly describe rape, concerns camps administered in Algeria. It does not describe conditions inside Western Sahara itself, and the sources do not establish whether comparable detention occurs within the territory.

The criminalisation figures reach the dossier through aggregation. The six-month-to-three-year range and the up-to-three-year Sahrawi figure come from secondary roundups and monitor entries rather than from primary text of the penal provisions, and no source quotes the operative statutory article for either framework. The current status of the constitution referred to in the 2010 statement, and whether any amendment has since added or removed protections, is not resolved here.
